title: Soneil International Ltd. (Aug 2011 TCC) SR&ED Ruling
subject: Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty, Hypothesis Testing and Records
summary: Soneil International Limited v. The Queen (2011 TCC 391) is a Tax Court of Canada decision in which Justice D'Arcy dismissed two appeals because the appellant corporations claiming SR&ED for 2002 wheelchair and scooter projects failed to prove technological uncertainty, systematic hypothesis testing and contemporaneous records, confirming the onus rests on the taxpayer.
metaDescription: Analyze the August 2011 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Soneil International Ltd. on Canadian R&D tax credit documentation.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Overview of the Claim

On August 19, 2011, Justice Steven K. D'Arcy of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) delivered the judgment in Soneil International Limited et al. v. The Queen, cited as 2011 TCC 391, 2011 DTC 1282, and [2011] TCJ No. 302 (QL). The judgment disposed of two appeals heard together on common evidence in Toronto on November 17, 18 and 19, 2010—one by Soneil International Limited ("International") and one by Soneil Usha Inc. ("Soneil")—both founded by Mr. Sachindra Jain, who started the business in the basement of his home in 1994 and brought to market the application of switch-mode technology in battery chargers, making them small, lightweight and suitable for onboard use in applications such as golf carts, material handling devices and scrubbing-cleaning devices, with battery-operated wheelchairs as the primary application; the products were developed in Canada, manufactured in China and Malaysia, and approximately 95% were sold outside Canada.

Each appellant appealed a notice of assessment for its 2002 taxation year under the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"); International's 2002 taxation year ended on September 30, 2002 and Soneil's on October 31, 2002, and the only issue before the Court was whether certain expenditures made by each appellant in that year constituted expenditures on Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED). The appellants claimed SR&ED for four projects relating to power wheelchairs and scooters: International's Power Optimization Project (a system to switch power between the front and rear wheels) and Inhibitor Project (a device to cut power to the wheels while the wheelchair is being charged), and Soneil's Virtual Battery Project (a method to deliver 36 volts from two 12-volt batteries) and Multi-voltage Project (a charger that senses the battery voltage of the specific wheelchair and charges at the appropriate voltage). The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") assessed each appellant on the basis that the work did not constitute SR&ED as defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA; at trial the Respondent called a Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), Mr. Yashvant Parmar, and an expert witness, Mr. Christopher Stoute, a consultant who had previously worked for the CRA and who in 2004 had prepared for the CRA a review report recommending that the appellants' SR&ED claim be denied.
Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

In the jurisdiction of Canada, tax incentives for research and development are governed by the interplay of three primary provisions within the ITA: subsection 248(1), which defines "scientific research and experimental development" (a definition formerly housed in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations); section 37, which establishes the pooling mechanism for deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada; and section 127, which governs the calculation of ITCs based on "qualified expenditures".

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For commercial industrial claimants such as Soneil International Limited, eligibility typically turns on paragraph (c) of the definition—experimental development—which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) permits support work (such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research) only where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) explicitly exclude routine activities, including market research, quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes, commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product, style changes, and routine data collection.

To operationalize the statutory language of subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the seminal five-question test articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), summarized by the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, at paragraph 17, and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), and relied upon by Justice D'Arcy at paragraph 13 of Soneil International. First, the Court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the inquiry examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the analysis determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, defined as an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological relations. Fifth, the Court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, was kept as the work progressed.
The Minister's Challenge and the Final Holding of the Tax Court of Canada

Before the Tax Court of Canada, where Mr. Jain appeared as agent for the appellants and was their only witness, the Minister's position was that the work on the four wheelchair and scooter power-system projects did not constitute SR&ED as defined in subsection 248(1), and the onus was on the appellants to show, on a balance of probabilities, that the expenditures were for SR&ED (paragraph 14). The Court ultimately found that the appellants had not provided sufficient evidence of a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures, nor of methodical and systematic testing of any hypothesis, and that they had not maintained a detailed record of the testing or its results as the work progressed (paragraphs 19–27).

Justice D'Arcy dismissed both appeals in respect of the 2002 taxation years and awarded costs to the Respondent, except that no costs were awarded with respect to her expert witness, whose report the Court considered "more in the nature of advocacy" than an expert report and to which it would have given no weight (paragraphs 40–43). In a holding that has since become a foundational authority in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence—repeatedly cited by the Tax Court of Canada in subsequent decisions such as R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 186) and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6)—Justice D'Arcy applied a strict evidentiary approach to, among other criteria, the third criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic test (the "scientific method" requirement).

Specifically, Justice D'Arcy noted at paragraph 14 of Soneil International that the onus is on the appellant to show, on a balance of probabilities, that its expenditures were for SR&ED as defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and concluded at paragraph 38 that the appellants did not provide sufficient evidence to support a finding that they adopted procedures that accorded with established and objective principles of scientific measure. In particular, the Court found that the appellants had not provided sufficient evidence that their work was characterized by three elements: trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the testing and modification of hypotheses. Because the appellants did not show, on a balance of probabilities, that their expenditures were for SR&ED, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed both appeals and found it unnecessary to consider the Respondent's evidence, including that of her expert witness (paragraph 41).
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Failure to Establish Systematic Investigation and Objective Scientific Measure

A central defect in Soneil International—alongside the appellants' failure to establish a technological uncertainty and their lack of contemporaneous records—was the appellants' inability to satisfy the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic: proving that the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of scientific measure. In Canadian tax litigation, tax assessments are presumed valid until demolished by the taxpayer through prima facie evidence. When a taxpayer claims that product development in an established engineering discipline (such as the battery charging and power systems for power wheelchairs at issue in Soneil International) constitutes SR&ED, the Court scrutinizes how the work was executed rather than merely looking at the commercial novelty of the finished product.

Justice D'Arcy emphasized that, after an appellant has identified the technological risk or uncertainty, it is important for it to provide evidence that it conducted methodical and systematic testing of any hypothesis designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty (paragraph 24). Although the decision does not prescribe a specific methodology, in practice demonstrating procedures that accord with objective principles of scientific measure typically requires the claimant to establish baseline parameters, control variables systematically, apply quantitative metrics to evaluate performance against theoretical predictions, and analyze the causal mechanisms of failure. In Soneil International, the appellants' documentary evidence consisted largely of single-page, point-form "systematic testing plans" (11 items for the Power Optimization Project; 9 items for the Inhibitor Project, 6 of which repeated the former; and 7 prototype requirements for the Multi-voltage Project), undated handwritten notes and simple diagrams of uncertain authorship, design diagrams that may have been produced by a Hong Kong company (Le Fronte), and a single-page "Test Report No 1" whose author Mr. Jain could not confirm; no analysis of specific tests or their results was filed for the Power Optimization or Inhibitor Projects (paragraphs 29–37). Without proof of rigorous measurement and controlled experimentation, the Court cannot distinguish claimed SR&ED from standard commercial product development or routine debugging.
Conflation of Routine Engineering and Standard Product Development with Technological Uncertainty

A recurring legal failure highlighted in Soneil International and related jurisprudence (including Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 549, which predates and was relied upon in Soneil International, and later decisions such as R&D Pro-Innovation and Joel Theatrical) is the conflation of a technical or commercial problem with a scientific or technological uncertainty. As noted in the jurisprudence citing Soneil International, commercial novelty, functional innovation, or building a product with better performance characteristics does not automatically equate to SR&ED.

Under Canadian law, a technological uncertainty exists only when the probability of achieving a given technical objective, or the path to achieving it, cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific knowledge or standard engineering practice. If an electronics manufacturer encounters heat dissipation issues, electromagnetic interference (EMI), or voltage regulation instability while designing a compact battery charger, resolving those issues by consulting component datasheets, applying standard electrical engineering formulas, or swapping off-the-shelf microcontrollers and MOSFETs constitutes "routine engineering". The first and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic are inextricably linked: where a taxpayer cannot articulate a genuine system-level technological constraint that defies standard engineering handbooks, the subsequent work inevitably manifests as trial-and-error troubleshooting rather than a hypothesis-driven systematic investigation.
Absence of Structured Hypothesis Formulation, Testing, and Modification

At paragraph 38 of Soneil International, Justice D'Arcy specifically found that the appellants had not provided sufficient evidence of "the testing and modification of hypotheses". In the legal context of subsection 248(1), a hypothesis is not a commercial goal (such as proposing that a firm can build a 24V battery charger that charges 20% faster). Rather, a valid scientific hypothesis is a testable, causal proposition explaining why a specific technological uncertainty exists and how manipulating specific independent variables will affect dependent physical or algorithmic parameters.

Furthermore, the requirement for the testing and modification of hypotheses underscores the iterative nature of experimental development. When an initial experiment fails to achieve the predicted metric, the scientific method requires the researcher to analyze the empirical measurement data, deduce why the underlying scientific assumption was incomplete or erroneous, formulate a modified hypothesis, and design a subsequent experiment. In Soneil International, the appellants lacked evidence of this progression: Mr. Jain acknowledged that he and his assistant did not keep detailed records, and testified that the assistant ran series of tests, many producing similar results, and that detailed tests were conducted once "change" was encountered, but he provided no evidence of encountering change, of what any change meant for a specific hypothesis, or of whether a change in the hypothesis was required (paragraph 27). The Court accepted that Mr. Jain and his assistant spent a significant amount of time working on upgrades to the appellants' products, but held that this did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the work constituted SR&ED (paragraph 16).
Evidentiary Deficiencies and Lack of Contemporaneous Documentation

While the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic (keeping detailed records of hypotheses tested and results as the work progresses) is technically an evidentiary guideline rather than a standalone statutory requirement in subsection 248(1), Soneil International and its progeny (R&D Pro-Innovation and Joel Theatrical) demonstrate that the absence of contemporaneous documentation is almost always fatal at trial.

In Soneil International, Justice D'Arcy focused directly on the insufficiency of the appellants' evidence, adopting Justice Little's statement in Zeuter (citing RIS-Christie) that the only reliable method of demonstrating that scientific research was undertaken in a systematic fashion is to produce documentary evidence (paragraph 25), and noting that Mr. Jain, a certified management accountant, clearly understood the importance of maintaining adequate records (paragraph 39). The only evidence of the alleged technological uncertainties was Mr. Jain's testimony at the November 2010 hearing about work performed in the 2002 taxation years, and his credibility was damaged on cross-examination when he had difficulty explaining emails that appeared to show a third-party manufacturer had redesigned the virtual battery units, and could not say whether documents he had presented as evidence of Soneil's testing were in fact design documents prepared by a Hong Kong company (paragraphs 19, 22 and 35). Although the decision does not list specific document types, in practice evidence capable of demonstrating "trained and systematic observation" and "measurement and experiment" includes dated lab notebooks, schematic revisions linked to specific failure analyses, oscilloscope waveforms, thermal imaging logs, test protocols, and quantitative datasets—in contrast to the handwritten notes with no sentences or detailed comments, of unknown authorship and date, that the Court rejected in Soneil International (paragraph 32). Filing high-level retroactive narratives on Form T661 or producing only final commercial drawings fails to prove the systematic nature of the intermediate investigation.
Ancillary Expenditure, Contractual, and Government Assistance Considerations

Beyond the threshold technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), Canadian SR&ED claimants operating in the commercial electronics and manufacturing sectors face strict statutory rules governing expenditure calculation and funding exclusions under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA. Claimants frequently receive federal or provincial grants or contributions, such as funding from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP); however, government assistance, contract payments and expenditure calculations were not at issue in Soneil International, where the only issue was whether the work constituted SR&ED under subsection 248(1) (paragraph 10). Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), any "government assistance" or "non-government assistance" that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED must be deducted from the qualified expenditure pool, reducing the base upon which the 35% enhanced CCPC ITC or 15% general ITC is calculated.

Similarly, to prevent double-dipping where a Canadian performer conducts SR&ED on behalf of another party, subsection 127(9) of the ITA excludes "contract payments" from the performer's qualified expenditures. If a company enters into a commercial contract where a customer pays for custom engineering or product development, and the contract either requires the performer to perform SR&ED or entitles the payer to the resulting intellectual property or performance, the CRA routinely characterizes the entire gross revenue of the contract as a "contract payment," eliminating the performer's ITC claim unless the contract is carefully structured as a standard commercial sale of goods rather than a contract for SR&ED services. Additionally, where corporate principals (who hold 10% or more of any class of shares, defined as "specified employees" under subsection 248(1)) perform SR&ED, their eligible salary is capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), bonuses and remuneration based on profits are strictly disallowed under subsection 37(9), and time spent on SR&ED versus commercial management must be substantiated by rigorous contemporaneous time-tracking.
Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements and Evidentiary Standards

The following table maps each governing Canadian statutory and jurisprudential requirement addressed in Soneil International Limited v. The Queen (2011 TCC 391) and related Tax Court of Canada authorities against the specific taxpayer deficiencies and the Court's mandated standard of proof.

headers: Taxpayer's Legal & Evidentiary Failure in Soneil International
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof

cells: 1. Existence of Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (ITA s. 248(1)(a)–(c))
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 1); Zeuter Development Corp. (2006 TCC 549); Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶17–22)

Described the uncertainties only as whether a "safe and effective" switchover system, inhibitor, virtual battery or multi-voltage charger could be developed and retrofitted for power wheelchairs; acknowledged that no new components were produced, that existing parts and components were used and that a wide body of knowledge already existed; and did not show that applying those components required more than routine engineering or standard procedures (¶18–22).

The taxpayer must adduce objective evidence establishing a system-level constraint or uncertainty that could not be resolved by a competent professional using standard engineering procedures, published datasheets, or routine design calculations.
2. Formulation of Specific Causal Hypotheses (ITA s. 248(1))
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶27, ¶38)

Filed single-page, point-form "systematic testing plans" listing specifications or prototype requirements rather than testable scientific propositions, and gave no evidence of what any change in results meant for a specific hypothesis or whether the hypothesis was modified (¶27, ¶29, ¶31, ¶36).

The taxpayer must prove that before each experimental cycle, a specific, falsifiable hypothesis was formulated linking independent design variables to dependent technical parameters aimed directly at removing the uncertainty.
3. Adoption of Objective Principles of Scientific Measure (ITA s. 248(1))
Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶38); R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. (2015 TCC 186, ¶32)

Relied on oral assertions of testing, a list of test equipment with few details of the testing facility, and undated handwritten notes, without filing any analysis of specific tests or their results (¶8, ¶30, ¶32–33).
The appellant must provide sufficient evidence to support a finding that it adopted procedures according with established and objective principles of scientific measure.
4. Three Pillars of the Scientific Method (ITA s. 248(1))
Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶38); Joel Theatrical (2017 TCC 6, ¶33–36)
Failed to demonstrate a structured experimental lifecycle connecting observation, quantitative data capture, failure analysis, and iterative re-testing.
Evidence must establish that work was characterized by: (1) Trained and systematic observation; (2) Measurement and experiment; and (3) Testing and modification of hypotheses.
5. Advancement in Scientific or Technological Knowledge (ITA s. 248(1)(c))
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Zeuter Development Corp.; R&D Pro-Innovation

Not specifically addressed: although Mr. Jain described a "technological advancement" for each project, the Court made no finding on this criterion because the appellants had already failed to prove a technological uncertainty and systematic testing (¶15–16, ¶38).

The taxpayer must demonstrate that the investigation generated new technological knowledge advancing the understanding of scientific relations, even if only an incremental advancement or a documented rejection of a hypothesis.
6. Contemporaneous Documentation of Systematic Investigation (ITA s. 248(1) & s. 230(1))
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶23–27, ¶38); Joel Theatrical (2017 TCC 6, ¶36)
Failed to file contemporaneous experimental logs, quantitative test matrices, or analytical records substantiating the intermediate steps of the investigation.
Self-serving retroactive oral testimony is insufficient; the taxpayer must produce contemporaneous documentary evidence (test logs, measured data, dated revisions) recorded as the work progressed.
7. Segregation of Support Work & Exclusion of Routine Testing (ITA s. 248(1)(d)–(k))
ITA s. 248(1)(d), (f), (i), (k); Soneil International (2011 TCC 391)

Not at issue in the decision: the Court did not address support work or the exclusions in paragraphs (e) to (k); it found only that the appellants had not shown that their work on upgrades to existing products, using existing parts and components, required more than routine engineering or standard procedures (¶16, ¶20–21).
Support work (engineering, design, programming, testing) is eligible under s. 248(1)(d) only if proved to be commensurate with the needs and directly in support of eligible experimental development.
8. Deductibility & Assistance / Contract Payment Adjustments (ITA s. 37(1), s. 127(9))
ITA s. 37(1)(d), s. 127(9), s. 127(18)–(20)

Not at issue in the decision (¶10); included as a general compliance consideration, since government grants (e.g., NRC-IRAP) or customer-funded engineering contracts that are not properly segregated from eligible pools can reduce ITCs.

Taxpayers must track labour and materials by specific SR&ED project, deduct government assistance (such as IRAP contributions), and structure commercial sales contracts to avoid "contract payment" clawbacks.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian taxpayers and their tax advisors can proactively operationalize the legal holdings of Soneil International Limited v. The Queen (2011 TCC 391), the following two industry case studies examine realistic commercial R&D projects vulnerable to the exact pitfalls identified by Justice D'Arcy. Each case study provides a step-by-step legal and technical remediation framework designed to withstand a CRA RTA review and Tax Court of Canada litigation.
Case Study 1: High-Frequency Switch-Mode Battery Charger and BMS Firmware Development in the Power Electronics Sector
Project Context and Inherited Soneil Pitfalls

VoltCore Power Systems Inc. ("VoltCore") is an Ontario-based CCPC manufacturing intelligent battery chargers and power management units for electric vehicles and industrial lithium-iron-phosphate (LiFePO₄) battery banks, broadly similar to the industry profile of Soneil International Limited, which developed switch-mode battery chargers used primarily in battery-operated wheelchairs. VoltCore undertakes a project to develop a compact, sealed, fanless onboard EV battery charger operating at a switching frequency of 500 kHz with an integrated Battery Management System (BMS) adaptive charging algorithm.

In an unremediated workflow falling into the Soneil International trap, VoltCore's engineers design a printed circuit board (PCB), build four prototype iterations over 14 months, encounter severe MOSFET thermal runaway and total harmonic distortion (THD) exceeding 8%, swap out inductors and thermal potting compounds until the unit passes CSA/UL certification, and file a Form T661 claiming 100% of the engineering team's salaries. Furthermore, VoltCore receives a $250,000 NRC-IRAP contribution toward the charger project and enters into a custom supply agreement with an electric motorcycle OEM that includes a "Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE)" fee. Under a CRA audit applying Soneil International (2011 TCC 391), the claim would be completely disallowed because VoltCore's documentation shows only schematic versions and final pass/fail certification tests, falling short of the evidence Justice D'Arcy found lacking in Soneil International, namely "trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the testing and modification of hypotheses".
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Isolating Technological Uncertainty from Routine Engineering

To satisfy Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic and address the deficiency identified at paragraphs 17–21 of Soneil International, VoltCore must establish a formal SR&ED Project Governance Charter prior to commencing experimental work. Rather than defining the project around the commercial product ("Develop a fanless EV charger"), the governance protocol must strictly segregate routine engineering from the core technological uncertainty. Schematic capture of standard input EMI filters, mechanical enclosure CAD modeling, standard PCB layout for auxiliary rails, and final CSA/UL safety certification testing are segregated into Commercial Cost Centre CC-100, as these activities constitute routine engineering or fall within the exclusions for quality control or routine testing and for commercial production in paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i) of the ITA.

Concurrently, the Lead Power Electronics Engineer documents a formal Baseline Literature and Technology Review at project inception to benchmark the existing scientific knowledge base. This document proves that using standard silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFET datasheets and conventional resonant LLC converter equations, increasing switching frequency to 500 kHz within a sealed, potted enclosure creates a coupled electromagnetic-thermal interaction: parasitic inter-winding capacitance (Cp) in the planar transformer induces high-frequency ringing that degrades Zero-Voltage Switching (ZVS) during light-load transitions, causing junction temperatures (Tj) to exceed 150 °C. Consequently, the technological uncertainty is formally logged as whether zero-voltage switching (ZVS) can be maintained across a wide output voltage range (40 V to 120 V) at 500 kHz without exceeding a MOSFET junction temperature of 125 °C and total harmonic distortion of 5%, given the spatial and thermal dissipation constraints of a hermetically potted enclosure where dielectric potting compound increases parasitic capacitance by 35% over air-insulated baselines.
Step 2: Implementing a Structured Process of Experimentation and Hypothesis Tracking

To address Justice D'Arcy's finding in Soneil International (¶38) that the appellants had not proved "the testing and modification of hypotheses," VoltCore replaces ad-hoc prototyping with a mandatory Hypothesis-Experiment-Modification (HEM) Protocol. Every experimental iteration is assigned a unique code in VoltCore's engineering repository (SR-EXP-01 through SR-EXP-08) and follows a four-stage scientific progression.

In the first stage, the team formulates an initial causal hypothesis (H<sub>1</sub>) proposing that if an interleaved dual-phase LLC resonant tank is configured with a magnetizing-to-resonant inductance ratio (L<sub>m</sub>/L<sub>r</sub>) of 6 and an asymmetric dead-time control algorithm modulated dynamically via drain-source voltage (V<sub>DS</sub>) sensing, then parasitic ringing energy induced by the high-permittivity silicone potting compound (ε<sub>r</sub> ≈ 3.0) will be reabsorbed into the resonant tank, reducing switching losses by 30% and keeping steady-state T<sub>j</sub> below 110 °C at 100% load. In the second stage, the team executes a controlled experimental design in which enclosure volume (1.2 L), potting compound thermal conductivity (1.5 W/m·K), and ambient temperature (40 °C) are held strictly constant, while varying only the L<sub>m</sub>/L<sub>r</sub> ratio (4, 6, 8) and dead-time window (50 ns to 200 ns) across three instrumented test boards.

In the third stage, empirical falsification and analytical evaluation of SR-EXP-01 demonstrate that while T<sub>j</sub> drops to 104 °C at full load (6.6 kW), when the battery reaches the Constant-Voltage (CV) tapering phase (≤ 20% load), the dielectric loss tangent (tan δ) of the potting compound shifts nonlinearly with temperature, causing phase-shedding instability and spiking current THD to 11%. Because H<sub>1</sub> is partially falsified, the team advances to the fourth stage—the modification of the hypothesis (H<sub>2</sub>)—directly addressing the deficiency identified at paragraph 38 of Soneil International. Under H<sub>2</sub>, the engineers hypothesize that replacing fixed threshold phase-shedding with a state-plane trajectory control law modeled by:

d<sub>t</sub>(k+1) = d<sub>t</sub>(k) + K<sub>ρ</sub> · [ρ<sub>ref</sub> − ρ(k)] − K<sub>C</sub> · (∂C<sub>p</sub>/∂T) · ΔT(k), where ρ(k) = √(v<sub>Cr</sub>(k)² + (Z<sub>0</sub> · i<sub>Lr</sub>(k))²)
that dynamically compensates for temperature-dependent capacitance drift will eliminate sub-harmonic oscillation during the CV charging taper and maintain THD below 5%.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Objective Measurement Protocols

To address the deficiency identified by Justice D'Arcy in Soneil International (¶38) regarding "trained and systematic observation" and "measurement and experiment" according with "established and objective principles of scientific measure", VoltCore institutes a mandatory Contemporaneous Evidence Archive. Every experimental run generates automated CSV data logs from a calibrated Yokogawa WT1800 power analyzer and multi-channel thermocouple data logger, recording switching frequency (f<sub>sw</sub>), efficiency (η), power factor (PF), THD, overshoot voltage, and junction temperatures (T<sub>j</sub>) at 10 ms intervals.

Furthermore, engineers are prohibited from overwriting firmware or modifying PCB hardware until a Hypothesis Closure Ticket is committed to the Git/Jira repository. Each ticket attaches before-and-after oscilloscope captures showing VDS and ID overlap, along with a written mathematical analysis explaining why the measured data diverged from the SPICE simulation model. Rather than relying on retroactive percentage estimates at year-end, all engineers and specified employees log hours daily against specific SR-EXP-XX tickets, separating eligible experimental analysis and commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) from commercial production support.
Step 4: Contractual Structuring, Subcontractor Agreements, and Government Assistance Reconciliation

To protect the financial integrity of the claim under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA, VoltCore maps the NRC-IRAP contribution agreement directly against its project tasks. To the extent the IRAP grant reimburses salaries claimed under SR&ED Project 1, VoltCore deducts the assistance on Form T661 Line 431 and Line 515 pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9). However, where the IRAP contribution agreement also funds commercial market readiness or non-SR&ED certification tasks housed in Cost Centre CC-100, VoltCore prepares a detailed Assistance Allocation Schedule demonstrating that the portion of IRAP funding attributable to non-SR&ED activities does not reduce the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool.

Simultaneously, to eliminate the "contract payment" trap on the electric motorcycle OEM agreement, legal counsel restructures the contract prior to execution instead of billing for "Custom R&D and Engineering Services to develop a charger," which would otherwise trigger a contract payment reduction under subsection 127(9). The agreement is drafted strictly as a Commercial Purchase Agreement for Deliverables (Modified Standard Hardware) at a fixed unit price for commercial units, explicitly stipulating that the purchaser is contracting solely for the delivery of physical battery charger units meeting functional commercial specifications, that the purchaser is neither contracting for nor requiring VoltCore to perform SR&ED, and that all background and foreground intellectual property, schematics, and experimental firmware remain the exclusive property of VoltCore.
Case Study 2: Electromechanical Actuator and Automated Override Control System in Heavy Industrial Manufacturing
Project Context and Inherited Soneil Pitfalls

Apex Rigging & Automation Ltd. ("Apex") is a Canadian mechanical and industrial engineering firm that designs and manufactures heavy-duty motorized winch, hoist, and automated kinetic rigging systems for large infrastructural and theatrical venues, analogous to the industrial equipment context in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 186, both of which directly applied Soneil International, 2011 TCC 391. Apex seeks to develop an ultra-quiet, dual-redundant electromechanical brake and manual-override planetary gear actuator capable of arresting a dynamic load moving at 2 m/s within a stopping distance of 300 mm, while restricting acoustic emissions to 65 dB(A) at 1 m and allowing seamless mechanical manual override during power failure without dangerous torque kickback.

In an unremediated scenario replicating the failures in Soneil International and Joel Theatrical, Apex's shop-floor machinists and mechanical engineers fabricate custom bronze and composite friction discs, machine three prototype gearboxes on the shop floor, test them by hanging weights in the warehouse and listening to the noise level, adjust spring tensions by feel until the manual override lever operates smoothly, and ultimately install the finished unit at a client's venue. At audit and trial, Apex submits CAD drawings of the final actuator and invoices for steel and machining. Applying Soneil International (2011 TCC 391, ¶14 and ¶38), the Tax Court of Canada would reject the claim in full because Apex failed to file any documents describing a systematic investigation, failed to establish objective principles of scientific measure by relying on subjective visual and auditory inspection rather than instrumented measurement, and built a commercial asset deployed directly in a customer contract.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Defining System-Level Technological Uncertainty

To avoid the fatal evidentiary collapse seen in Soneil International and Joel Theatrical, Apex implements a strict Stage-Gate Technical Governance Framework before cutting any metal. Legal and technical advisors train the engineering team on the rule affirmed in Zeuter, R&D Pro-Innovation, and Soneil International: mechanical novelty or clever design of a manual override mechanism does not constitute SR&ED unless resolving an underlying technological uncertainty requires systematic experimentation.

The Lead Mechanical Engineer documents the exact conflict between governing physical principles that cannot be resolved via standard machinery handbooks. Specifically, achieving a 300 mm arrest distance for a 2,000 kg load at 2 m/s requires dissipating 4 kJ of kinetic energy in 0.3 s, demanding high clamp force and high static and dynamic friction coefficients (μ ≥ 0.4). However, high-μ metallic friction interfaces under rapid engagement generate stick-slip tribological excitation between 1 kHz and 4 kHz (exceeding 85 dB(A)), whereas elastomeric damping layers that attenuate noise below 65 dB(A) suffer viscoelastic shear failure and thermal glaze under 4 kJ energy spikes. Furthermore, coupling a manual override cam to a high-ratio planetary stage under residual torsional wind-up creates unpredictable back-driving torque spikes (up to 450 N·m) during clutch disengagement.
Step 2: Implementing a Structured Process of Experimentation and Hypothesis Tracking

To address the three elements Justice D'Arcy found lacking in Soneil International (¶38)—trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and testing and modification of hypotheses—Apex structures its investigation around formal Experimental Test Protocols (ETP). Prior to fabrication, the engineering team formulates a testable hypothesis (H<sub>1</sub>) stating that by machining micro-textured sinusoidal grooves (wavelength λ = 2 mm, depth d = 0.15 mm) into a carbon-ceramic rotor paired with a constrained-layer viscoelastic damping ring bonded to the stator backplate, interfacial shear waves generated during a 2 m/s emergency arrest will undergo destructive acoustic interference, maintaining acoustic emission below 65 dB(A) while preserving a stable dynamic friction coefficient of 0.42 ± 0.03 across interface temperatures from 20 °C to 350 °C.

Instead of building a full commercial winch for a client, Apex executes ETP-01 by constructing an instrumented Experimental Dynamometer Test Bench in a dedicated R&D bay, systematically testing ten coupon rotors with varying groove geometries (λ, d) and three viscoelastic polymer formulations across 50 arrest cycles each. Empirical data from ETP-01 reveals that while H<sub>1</sub> suppresses acoustic output to 62 dB(A) during the first 12 cycles, worn carbon-ceramic debris accumulates in the micro-grooves by cycle 15, causing sudden tribological lockup and inducing a 380 N·m torsional rebound into the manual override planetary carrier.

With H<sub>1</sub> empirically falsified, the team formulates a modified hypothesis (H<sub>2</sub>) consistent with paragraph 38 of Soneil International. Under H<sub>2</sub>, the engineers propose that introducing logarithmic spiral evacuation channels pitched at 30° relative to the radial vector, coupled with a two-stage progressive-rate Belleville washer stack pre-loaded according to the nonlinear stiffness relation:
F(δ) = k<sub>1</sub> · δ + k<sub>3</sub> · δ³, with k<sub>1</sub> = 1.8 kN/mm for stage 1 (δ ≤ 0.6 mm) and k<sub>1</sub> = 4.2 kN/mm for stage 2 (0.6 mm < δ ≤ 1.2 mm)
will continuously evacuate third-body wear debris via centrifugal shear while linearizing the torque release curve during manual override engagement to within ±5% of nominal release torque.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Objective Measurement Protocols

To eliminate the evidentiary deficit that doomed the taxpayers in Soneil International and Joel Theatrical, Apex bans subjective observations ("brake was quieter," "override lever felt smoother") from project records and mandates strict objective measurement across every dynamometer test cycle. Acoustic and vibration spectra from 20 Hz to 20 kHz are captured using a Class 1 integrating sound level meter and piezoelectric accelerometers generating Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) plots. Dynamic braking torque (Tb) and manual override release torque (Tr) are recorded at a 10 kHz sampling rate via an inline rotary torque transducer, while stopping distance (s) is measured to ±0.1 mm precision using high-speed optical encoders alongside infrared pyrometry logging rotor surface temperature profiles (Ts). All raw sensor files are automatically timestamped and uploaded to an immutable cloud engineering database alongside a Test Synthesis Matrix linking each hypothesis (Hn), independent variable settings, measured empirical outputs, statistical variance, and engineering conclusions.
Step 4: Contractual Structuring, Shop-Floor Cost Segregation, and Compliance Architecture

Because commercial production and experimental development frequently overlap in heavy manufacturing, Apex implements rigorous legal and accounting safeguards governing materials, shop-floor labour, and customer contracts. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the cost of materials may be claimed for SR&ED only if they are "materials consumed" (rendered virtually valueless) or "materials transformed" in the prosecution of SR&ED. If Apex builds an experimental actuator and subsequently installs or sells that physical unit to a commercial customer, the CRA will disallow the material costs or trigger a Recapture of Investment Tax Credit under subsections 127(27) through (35) when the property is converted to commercial use. To prevent this, Apex designates the Experimental Dynamometer Test Bench and all test rotors and gearboxes under Project Code SR-MECH-02 as Dedicated Experimental Scrap/Prototypes, scrapping the destructive test coupons once testing concludes and documenting the disposal via dated scrap certificates and photographs.

Concurrently, machinists and shop technicians log time using barcode scanners at the CNC and dynamometer stations. Time spent machining experimental test coupons (ETP-01, ETP-02) is booked to the SR&ED work order as directly commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d), whereas time spent fabricating the subsequent commercial production units for the customer is booked strictly to Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). Finally, in its customer contract for the venue rigging system, Apex separates the commercial supply and installation agreement from its internal R&D program, specifying standard performance requirements and fixed commercial pricing for delivered rigging hardware so that Apex acts as an independent manufacturer selling a commercial product rather than a service provider paid to conduct SR&ED on the customer's behalf.

The table below synthesizes the exact legal, technical, and accounting controls implemented in Case Studies 1 and 2 to overcome the judicial barriers established in Soneil International Limited v. The Queen (2011 TCC 391).

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Practice Directives for Canadian SR&ED Claimants

The decision of Justice D'Arcy in Soneil International Limited v. The Queen (2011 TCC 391) stands as a watershed evidentiary precedent in Canadian SR&ED tax law. By applying the statutory phrase "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and concluding that the appellants had not provided sufficient evidence that their work was characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the testing and modification of hypotheses, or that they adopted procedures that accorded with established and objective principles of scientific measure, the Tax Court of Canada signaled that claims substantiated merely by point-form specifications, undated notes of uncertain authorship, and oral testimony given years after the work will not discharge the taxpayer's onus.

For Canadian corporations, in-house engineering directors, and tax counsel, defending an SR&ED claim before the CRA and the Tax Court of Canada requires integrating legal compliance directly into the engineering workflow from the first day of a project. Claimants must institutionalize pre-experiment baseline literature reviews to isolate genuine technological uncertainties from routine engineering, enforce mandatory quantitative instrumentation during every experimental iteration, archive dated records of falsified and modified hypotheses, and structure commercial customer contracts and government assistance agreements to protect the resulting qualified expenditure pool under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA.
